data.title: Trump: Iran war will be over 'sort of whenever I want it to be'
data.description:
President Trump said the Iran war would be over “sort of whenever I want it to be” as the conflict nears its ninth month and pushback against it grows. 

The president called soldiers at Mar-a-Lago on Thursday alongside first lady Melania Trump, saying they “joined millions of Americans this holiday to pray for your safety and success, and you continue.”

“You’re going to continue that deployment, and we have victory at hand,” he stated. “It’s going to be whenever, sort of, whenever I want it to be, to be honest.”

“We’re trying to be nice…we’re giving them every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives,” he continued. “But I’m not sure if they are going to take advantage of that. Some people question why. Are they crazy? Maybe they are.” 

As Democrats prepare to take the majorities in both chambers of Congress, Trump faces increasing pressure to end the conflict with Iran. Senate Republicans defeated a resolution earlier this month that would have directed Trump to end hostilities in the Middle East.

In the past month, Iran and the U.S. have engaged in tit-for-tat attacks as both countries face pressure domestically to end the conflict. Iranian strikes targeted a U.S. air base in Kuwait, while American forces struck Tehran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz following an unofficial quiet period of roughly two months. 

Two oil tankers were also struck by naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard navy said in a statement, according to state media. The Guard navy accused the tankers of trying to use a route that avoided Iranian control of the strait. 

The conflict’s cost reportedly rose to just more than $47 billion in October, though recently Arthur Miller, the deputy comptroller for budget and appropriations affairs at the Pentagon, told Senators on the Senate Armed Services Committee hearing that the updated cost of the Iran war was $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13.

data.title: Trump signals further openness to working with Democrats on healthcare
data.description:
President Trump signaled an increased openness to working with Democrats on healthcare after the party’s sweeping victories in the midterms, taking control of the House and Senate.

“I have a feeling we’re going to end up with a very bipartisan relationship with the Democrats,” Trump told reporters while at Mar-a-Lago.

“I hope so, where we can take care of a lot of different things, healthcare and so many other things, and get them done,” the president stated.

Trump said Democrats were reaching out to avoid his veto power, which the president signaled he didn’t want to use.

“It’s a very strong power. You have the power of veto, the power of pardon. They’re very, very strong,” he expressed. “They say in many ways they’re the most powerful thing a president has, and I’m not looking to veto everything for two years, and that’s not what they want either.”

“I have a feeling we’re going to have a great relationship, and a lot of things are going to get done,” he concluded. “Maybe more than would have gotten done the more traditional way. It’s happened before.”

While Trump floated working with Democrats on healthcare, he later followed up, saying he was going to “veto, veto, veto until we get legislation that’s going to be great for everybody.”

Expanding healthcare coverage became a campaign promise for many incoming lawmakers, particularly Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.). The incoming senator advocated for a single-payer healthcare bill — commonly referred to as Medicare for All — that he said he would rebrand to “Trumpcare,” in order to garner the president’s support. 

Trump re-shared to Truth Social a social media post El-Sayed made earlier this month, featuring photos of gold-plated “TrumpCare” cards.

El-Sayed on Sunday told NBC News’s Kristen Welker that he didn’t care what it was called, as his “job is to make sure that we’re advancing the goal to get everybody in this country healthcare.”

“Now, I don’t really care what it’s called. I care that the people of this country finally have the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country,” he stated during his “Meet the Press” interview.

Trump announced the pair are expected to meet regarding El-Sayed’s “Medicare for All” plan, though it is unclear when the meeting is scheduled. 

Trump has been able to work with Democrats on certain COVID-funding packages during his first term, when Republicans only controlled the Senate.

data.title: El-Sayed shares how to navigate 'spicier' Thanksgiving conversations
data.description:
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) shared a video Thursday on how to navigate “spicier” Thanksgiving conversations.

“Hey friends, I know Thursday is Thanksgiving and it’s an opportunity to come together and break bread with people with whom you might not have had a lot of conversations in the past,” he said in a video posted on social platform X. “And sometimes those conversations can get, well, let’s say a little bit spicier than the Thanksgiving meal. And I know that this is cause for a lot of anxiety.”

He recommended a habit he picked up while on the campaign trail, which was to invite people to reach out to others beyond politics.

“The things that we all agree on: the importance of the loved ones in our lives, our pets, whether or not you think the Lions are going to win on Thanksgiving Day,” the incoming senator said. 

El-Sayed blamed President Trump for the reason behind having conversations about life because he believed the president forced “us to take sides.”

“And so as you’re thinking and preparing for those conversations, sometimes maybe it’s not worth having. But if it is, I hope that you’ll find the place of agreement, the things that unite us rather than divide us,” he continued. 

The incoming senator expressed he believed it was important to find “the things that we agree on, that helps us to address where we disagree in a much more agreeable way.”

“So as you prepare for that sometimes anxiety-provoking conversation over Thanksgiving with that uncle that you don’t see eye to eye with, I hope that you’ll take it as an opportunity to find the places that you agree on, and maybe build from there,” he concluded. 

The incoming senator recently found some common ground with Trump on expanding healthcare access. The president told reporters he planned to meet with El-Sayed about a single-payer healthcare bill — also known as “Medicare for All” — which El-Sayed renamed “TrumpCare.”

data.title: Petition to oust US ambassador reaches Canadian Parliament
data.description:
A petition signed by nearly 290,000 Canadians calling on Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government to expel U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra was formally presented to Canada’s House of Commons on Thursday.

Canadian Green Party leader Elizabeth May introduced the nonbinding petition, which urged the government to declare President Trump’s ambassador “persona non grata” and revoke his diplomatic privileges in the country.

“He has been repeatedly abusive and insulting to Canadians,” May said of Hoekstra to Politico, describing him as “the most undiplomatic diplomat” Canada has ever seen.

“And with that, I wish him a happy Thanksgiving,” she added. “I think there are other countries he’d be happier living in.”

The petition, initiated by a Calgary resident, accuses Hoekstra of interfering in Canadian political affairs and undermining diplomatic relations between the two countries by propping up Trump’s push to make Canada the 51st U.S. state.

The Canadian government is required to formally respond to petitions presented in the House of Commons but is under no obligation to act on its demands.

Hoekstra, a former Republican congressman from Michigan and longtime Trump ally, has repeatedly drawn criticism from Canadian officials over his defense of the president’s rhetoric and policies toward the neighboring country.

In June, the ambassador said Trump and Carney should have a “great discussion” about Canada becoming the 51st state, months after Trump referred to Carney as the “future governor of Canada,” reviving a label he frequently used against former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau.

Hoekstra has also criticized Canadian politicians over their opposition to Trump’s tariffs and warned earlier this year that the countries’ defense relationship could change if Canada abandoned its planned purchase of American-made F-35 fighter jets.

Despite the backlash, the ambassador has maintained relationships with several Canadian provincial leaders, including Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Ontario Premier Doug Ford.

Hoekstra has previously dismissed concerns about his popularity among Canadians.

“It’s not about me, OK. Donald Trump did not tell me to go to Canada and become liked,” Hoekstra told Politico earlier this year. “Matter of fact, I think he would have said, ‘If you go to Canada and you’re liked, it probably means that you’re not doing your job.’”

data.title: Mexican leader rebukes US over DEA tip lines, claims 'interference'
data.description:
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum rebuked U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration officials over its tip line, claiming it interfered with her country’s work. 

“The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot,” Sheinbaum stated, according to the Associated Press. “The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States linked to organized crime, or what they call terrorist groups.”

The Mexican president’s remarks came after she read parts of an Associated Press report, published on Tuesday, that alleged the DEA chose not to seize at least 1.4 million counterfeit fentanyl pills while it tracked a drug trafficking ring for eight months. Amid the DEA’s inaction, the deadly drugs eventually flooded into the Southwest.

President Trump has attempted to pressure Sheinbaum to crack down on suspected cartel activity, while she accused him of undermining her leadership.

DEA Administrator Terry Cole also recently announced a tip line that encouraged people to report “members and associates of designated Foreign Terrorist Organizations (FTOs). Corrupt government officials providing material support to designated FTOs. Criminal networks and individuals laundering money to finance narcoterrorism.”

“Your information matters. Your identity and safety matter,” Cole wrote. “If you have information, connect with the DEA through the designated reporting channels.”

“Together, we can expose corruption, disrupt financial networks, dismantle narcoterrorist organizations, and protect our communities,” he concluded. 

Sheinbaum asserted on Monday that U.S. officials were not allowed to operate on Mexican soil after it was discovered that the military flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to assist in capturing a top Sinaloa drug lord. 

Authorities arrested Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, also known as “El Chapo Isidro,” who was on the FBI’s most wanted list. He was accused of manufacturing and distributing a large amount of methamphetamine, cocaine, heroin and marijuana, along with illegally possessing and using a firearm.

“This case in particular demonstrates the capacity of the armed forces” of Mexico to make major detentions, Sheinbaum said, per the Associated Press.

data.title: Democrats' plan to end funding for Iran war leaves open what comes next
data.description:
One of the top priorities for the incoming Democratic majorities is cutting off funding for the U.S. war with Iran, which was launched by President Trump nine months ago with no input from Congress. 

What happens after that — and whether Democrats can force Trump to end the war without jeopardizing U.S. forces in the region — remains an open question. 

 “We’re working on a consensus position; we’re not there yet,” Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), a member of the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, told The Hill. 

“We’re not there yet. It will be soon.”

One of the first opportunities for Democrats to throttle offensive operations in Iran is coming up even before they retake control of the House and Senate. Congress faces a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government, which some Democrats see as an opportunity. 

A full-year spending bill with Republican support would likely preserve funding for the war at a precarious time, when Trump is alternating between threats to restart offensive military operations and to hold out with sanctions and a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz. 

Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), the ranking member of the House Appropriations Committee, has said she’s in favor of full-year spending bills for as many uncontroversial funding priorities as possible.

That could leave open the option for a short-term spending bill on the military, with Democrats addressing the war when they take over the majority in Congress in January.

“To a person, we all want to see the funding on the war ended; the issue is how that gets done, what we can do in the short term and then what we need to do afterward,” DeLauro told reporters last week.

The immediate path forward on Iran is not expected to become clear until after Senate Democrats vote on their caucus leadership Dec. 1. 

The contest is between longtime leader Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who has elevated his progressive bona fides over the past few years. This includes his challenging the Biden administration’s policy on Israel.

Van Hollen has called for “not one penny more” in funding for the war. Schumer’s position is unclear.

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), who is backing Schumer, along with Sens. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), who are undecided, announced last week they will move to add an amendment to appropriations bills to block funding for the Iran war.

“This amendment is the bare minimum Congress can do to heed Americans’ call and use our power of the purse to force the President to end this conflict we never should’ve been in,” Duckworth said in a statement. 

Some House Democrats also see ending funds for the war immediately as increasing pressure on Trump to pursue diplomacy with Tehran. 

“If we end the war, it will force Trump to the negotiating table with Iran,” said Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), a member of the House Armed Services Committee. 

Sen. Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said the U.S. needs to advance a diplomatic resolution with Iran. 

“The administration needs to come and talk with us and consult with us, and as they continue to work on a diplomatic solution, we all need to be engaged,” she said. 

The challenge for Democrats will be preserving funding for the defense of U.S. troops in appropriations bills without letting the administration use those resources for offensive operations on Iran.

“Crafting the language that an administration can’t drive a truck through, and find a loophole, is hard. But I do think it is important,” said Damian Murphy, senior vice president for national security and international policy at the Center for American Progress. 

Funding for defense of allies and partners is also a bipartisan priority. But ending funding for major bombing campaigns is important, Murphy argued, blocking the administration from relying on what’s proven to be a failed strategy. 

“This idea that you can somehow bomb your way to what you want, this administration has had nine months of time to do that … and it just hasn’t worked,” he said. 

“As you look at the ledger, the answer is pretty clear that the first thing that needs to happen is an end to these kinetic operations and a focus on a serious diplomatic pressure track.”

The war is stuck in a fragile and dangerous stalemate. Trump has held off renewing large-scale bombing campaigns amid concerns over munitions shortages for defense for both U.S. assets in the region and Persian Gulf and Arab partners.

Sanctions and the U.S. naval blockade against Iran have helped increase the economic pressure on Iran and allow for some ships to move through the Strait of Hormuz. But danger is ever-present and escalating.

Two oil tankers struck naval mines, causing explosions and fires, in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard navy said in a statement carried by state media. The Guard navy accused the tankers of trying to use a route that avoided Iranian control of the strait. 

The mine collisions come as attacks on tankers reached their highest levels in October with 30 ships damaged, CNN reported, and at least 22 attacks on ships in the first three weeks of November.

The persistent attacks on oil tankers are keeping oil prices high, The Wall Street Journal reported, adding that even as other export routes come online, oil price per barrel is expected to be between $85 and $95 — keeping prices high at the pump. 

Iran is further projecting defiance, launching limited strikes against U.S. military installations in the Persian Gulf, particularly in Bahrain in recent days. The top commander of the Guard, Maj. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi, said in a speech Wednesday that Iran is ready to “drive the enemy” into retreat, according to state-backed media. 

Who is leading diplomacy on the U.S. side is up in the air, although it remains fully under Trump’s control. 

“Congress can make recommendations and can suggest ideas on that front, can demand oversight on how the diplomacy is going,” Murphy said. “But they can’t actually conduct the diplomacy itself.”

Trump announced earlier this month that he was removing Vice President Vance from talks on the war, after Vance blamed the Republican midterm losses on the conflict. 

Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s close friend and his son-in-law, respectively, have turned their attention away from Iran and toward negotiating an end to Russia’s war in Ukraine. However, the duo reportedly discussed Iran with senior Qatari officials last week in Berlin on the sidelines of meetings about Ukraine. 

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser, has often stayed on the sidelines of the conflict. But he’s increased the pace of calls with Persian Gulf partners in recent days, speaking with his counterparts in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain by phone and holding a meeting with the Qatari prime minister and foreign minister in Washington on Tuesday. 

Rubio would be an effective Iran czar but has held back from asserting himself, argued Michael Makovsky, president and CEO of the Jewish Institute for National Security of America.

“He’s the most knowledgeable of any of them. He’s been dealing with the Iran issue for a long time. I think he’s purposely tried not to be out ahead on Iran,” Makovsky said. “My understanding is internally he’s not overly assertive, but he should be.”

data.title: Thanksgiving storms ground DC flights, knock out power for over 850K
data.description:
A powerful coastal storm disrupted Thanksgiving travel in the Washington, D.C., area on Thursday as heavy rain and winds stopped flights at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

Along the East Coast, hundreds and thousands of homes and businesses lost power, along with more in the Midwest.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a ground stop temporarily at DCA due to thunderstorms.

The agency also warned of potential ground stops at Washington Dulles International Airport and Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport in Maryland through the evening.

More than 420 flights had been canceled nationwide and nearly 2,000 flights were delayed by late Thursday afternoon, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware, with airports serving Washington and New York City among the hardest hit.

Most major airlines have issued travel waivers for the affected Thanksgiving flights, including United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, American Airlines and JetBlue.

Meanwhile, more than 850,000 utility customers were without electricity nationwide as of 5 p.m. EST, according to PowerOutage.us, with Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania accounting for more than half of the outages.

More than 178,000 customers in Virginia and 174,000 in Maryland were without power, while Pennsylvania recorded roughly 154,000 outages. Another 86,000 customers in New Jersey and nearly 20,000 in Delaware faced electricity outages.

Water customers in the Maryland suburbs of D.C. were asked by Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission to conserve water in the face of power outages at filtration plants at midafternoon Thursday.

The National Weather Service (NWS) reported wind gusts of between 50 and 70 mph across portions of the East Coast including Virginia, Maryland, New York and coastal New England.

The threat of severe weather prompted officials to postpone the 100th annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday, making the first weather-related postponement in the event’s history.

The parade is now scheduled to take place at 8:30 a.m. EST Saturday, which New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) will miss because he is scheduled to have surgery Friday on his right leg after tearing his Achilles tendon.

data.title: Emmer: GOP should have said it wasn't 'realistic' to fix economy in 2 years
data.description:
House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) said Republicans should have spent the past two years tempering voters’ expectations about how quickly President Trump could turn the economy around, acknowledging that the party ceded the issue of affordability to Democrats ahead of its bruising midterm losses.

“We need to take responsibility for our messaging. We did not listen to the American people,” Emmer said Tuesday in an interview with Fox 9 Minneapolis.

“When we became the majority with the Senate and the White House, the idea that you were going to fix an economy that had been destroyed under [former President] Joe Biden in two years was not realistic,” he continued. “We should have been sticking with that economic message from day one, and we didn’t do it.”

The Minnesota Republican added that Democrats “did talk to those issues when they talked about affordability,” which resonated with voters who then voted Democrats back into power in the House and Senate.

His remarks come as Republicans reckon with losing both chambers of Congress, leaving Trump without unified Republican control in the legislative branch for the final two years of his presidency.

Emmer, who won a seventh term representing Minnesota’s 6th Congressional District earlier this month, will serve as minority whip in the next Congress. He signaled a willingness to work with Democrats but questioned whether the incoming majorities would follow through on their campaign promises to bring down costs.

“There should be a joint effort to resolve these problems,” he said. “The new Democrat majorities that are coming in, they campaigned on affordability, but that’s what they’re going to have to deliver. And right now, it doesn’t look like that’s what their focus is.”

The Minnesota Republican also weighed in on the war with Iran, describing the nine-month conflict as a “stalemate” despite Trump’s repeated declarations of victory. He defended the president’s efforts to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon but stressed the need to bring the conflict to an end and restore peace in the region.

“When it comes to the war, if it is a war, I don’t know what it is right now — it seems more like a stalemate,” he said.

Looking ahead to the next election cycle in 2028, Emmer said Republicans need to give Americans a reason to vote for them.

“I think the bigger issue for Republicans is we need to reestablish our identity as to who we are and what we offer,” he said. “We got to be for something.”

data.title: Musk pledges 2 SpaceX shares per American child
data.description:
SpaceX and its CEO Elon Musk announced Wednesday that they would each donate a share of the aerospace company’s stock to every American child with an active “Trump Account,” doubling a pledge the billionaire made last month.

The company said in a statement it would issue new shares of its Class A common stock to those with active Trump Accounts, an investment account for American children that helps build long-term savings. Musk also intends on personally matching the stocks donated by SpaceX.

“SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary,” the company said. “We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit.”

Musk said in a Thursday post on the social platform X that SpaceX would distribute its shares next month.

“The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year,” he added.

SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell previously pledged to donate more than 2 million shares of the company’s stock through the program. The gift will go to children from low-income areas between the ages of 11 and 17, primarily focusing on those who live near her home in central Texas.

The announcement comes after the Treasury Department said Tuesday that friends and family members had contributed more than $1 billion to individual Trump Accounts, bringing the total deposits in President Trump’s child investment program to more than $9 billion.

Nearly 70 million accounts have been established under the program, including more than 60 million through the administration’s automatic enrollment initiative announced in October.

The tax-advantaged investment accounts were established under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Trump signed into law in July 2025. Children younger than 18 with valid Social Security numbers are eligible for accounts. Those born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028 — the duration of Trump’s second term in office — qualify for a one-time $1,000 contribution from the federal government.

The program has attracted billions of dollars in philanthropic commitments, including a $6.25 billion pledge from Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell and his wife, Susan Dell, to provide $250 to children living in ZIP codes with a median family income of $150,000 or less.

data.title: Trump unloads on critics in wide-ranging Thanksgiving Day rant
data.description:
President Trump marked Thanksgiving Day with a lengthy rant on social media in which he lashed out at his political opponents, accused federal officials of releasing “fake” economic numbers and called for the mass expulsion of Somalis from the U.S.

In a grievance-filled post on Truth Social, the president began by wishing Americans a happy Thanksgiving holiday before turning his attention to his call for an investigation into economic data released ahead of the midterm elections.

“I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated,” Trump wrote.

The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) said Wednesday that the economy grew at an annualized rate of 4.3 percent between July and September, up from its initial estimate of 3.4 percent.

Trump alleged without evidence that the initial gross domestic product (GDP) estimates were deliberately understated and called for an investigation into the figures earlier Thursday after Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate in a midterm election cycle dominated by voters’ concerns over inflation and the rising cost of living.

GDP estimates are routinely revised as more comprehensive data becomes available. The BEA is scheduled to release another estimate next month.

Trump also accused Democrats and the “Radical Far Left” of seeking to impose Sharia law in the U.S. court system and force Americans to redistribute their money “so that all of the hardworking people that have built up, over a lifetime, a certain Wealth, will now be forced to distribute it throughout the Country, even to those who refuse to work.”

The president then turned his attention the Somali community, claiming without evidence that a fraction of the country’s Somali population works without receiving federal aid.

“I want to thank the 2% of our Somalian population that have a job, and are actually willing to work, without receiving Government Assistance,” he wrote. “These are wonderful American ‘citizens,’ and should be allowed to stay in our Country, and celebrate Thanksgiving with us. The others should be thrown out, immediately.”

Trump has repeatedly disparaged Minnesota’s Somali community amid federal investigations into widespread fraud involving government-funded social services programs in the state.

The president also touted his renovations to the White House, ripping the media and others who have criticized his changes to the complex, including the construction of a massive ballroom in the East Wing.

“I took time out of my very busy schedule to fix the 17 broken windows, numerous chipped and decaying columns, broken, dilapidated, and missing moldings, and lack of a proper plaster and paint job on the White House,” he wrote. “Today, it has never looked better, and will soon have the Ballroom that Presidents have sought for over 150 years.”
